I should have protected others and I failed

vignette:
Ravi was thirty-four when he deployed as a relief worker in a conflict zone, part of a team that delivered medical supplies to a besieged town. The attack came without warning: mortar fire hit the convoy, and the vehicle ahead burst into flames. He dragged two wounded colleagues from the wreckage, but a third was trapped. The smoke and the screaming-he can still feel the heat on his face, the way his body froze when he realized he could not reach her. The sequence of those minutes is a jumble; he knows he carried someone, then ran, then fell, but the order makes no sense. What stays sharp is the shame: he should have found a way. The world he believed in-orderly, decent-collapsed with that explosion.

Months after returning home to his wife and his job as a tax consultant, Ravi learned that the world had not repaired itself. A neighbor's barbecue sent smoke curling over the fence, and his chest tightened, his hands flew to his face. He could feel himself pinned again, legs unable to move. Smells-any faint whiff of burning-unleashed disjointed images and a bodily reenactment that left him trembling. Funerals became unbearable; he skipped his uncle's service because the sight of a grave would trigger the confused, shame-laden fragments. Even calm expressions of anger in the office-a client's firm tone-made him feel the heat of that day, reinforcing his conviction that danger lurked beneath ordinary surfaces. Each trigger confirmed his shattered belief that the world is fundamentally unsafe and that he failed the one person he was supposed to protect.

At night Ravi cannot settle; he checks the locks repeatedly, startles at the furnace clicking on, and lies rigid, listening. That constant vigilance meant that the furnace's click-a sound he had once ignored-now felt like an intrusion, each time pulling him back into the memory because his body was already primed for danger. His concentration at work has frayed-miscounting figures, misplacing files-because his mind is always scanning for threat. The hypervigilance itself drags him back into the traumatic moment: a sudden sound, and his body tenses into that same crouch behind the burning vehicle. The shame then surges anew, and with it the thought that he is permanently set apart from people who have not seen what he saw. He has come to believe that he does not deserve happiness, so he declines invitations to gatherings that might lift his mood-birthday parties, a colleague's promotion celebration-because experiencing joy would feel like betrayal. His wife notices him turning away from her attempts at comfort, but Ravi cannot explain that smiling feels wrong.

In the evenings he avoids the news entirely, especially any report from that region, as if staying away keeps the memories contained. Yet the avoidance backfires: he never sees the images, so the chaotic fragments remain unchallenged and the shame deepens. When a trigger does break through-a client's raised voice, a whiff of smoke-he covers his face with both hands, a gesture that momentarily cuts off the world but also prevents him from testing whether the threat is real. That covering, he believes, is the only thing that keeps him from falling apart; instead, it leaves him more convinced that he cannot cope, and the next trigger becomes even more potent. The cycle tightens: the more he hides, the more his body stays on alert, and the more his memory stays fractured and raw.

What finally brought Ravi to seek help was his wife's quiet plea after he missed his own anniversary dinner because she had lit a scented candle-the smell, he said, was wrong. He could not explain why a candle felt like a funeral pyre. Now he sits in the therapist's office, hands clasped, staring at the floor. He is afraid that telling the story will bring the shame back, that he will be judged as weak, that the confused fragments will never form a straight line. But he is more afraid of losing the life he still has. He hopes, without really believing it, that someone can help him feel less alone.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not clearly show that Ravi's sense of threat (hypervigilance) causes triggers to appear or become more potent; instead, triggers lead to threat.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly show that Ravi's sense of threat (hypervigilance) causes triggers to appear or become more potent; instead, triggers lead to threat.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
